passage: Payal had posted the plan for Vandana's surprise birthday in the class group chat at nine. By lunch, only four of twenty had replied. The read receipts showed Vandana's cousin had seen it and said nothing. Payal felt a tightness in her chest. Were people annoyed? Bored? She started drafting a message, "Guys?? Anyone?", then deleted it. Her friend Meera reminded her, "Half of them are in practicals till four." Payal put the phone in her bag. At five, the replies came in a rush: two offering to bring snacks, one apologising for the delay. The silence had been schedules, not disapproval. She still felt a little foolish, and also relieved she had not sent the message.

qa.q: How many of twenty had replied by lunch?
qa.a: Four of twenty had replied.

qa.q: What did Payal fear the silence meant, and what did it turn out to be?
qa.a: She feared people were annoyed or bored, but it turned out that they were busy in practicals.

qa.q: What could Payal do next time a group is slow to answer?
qa.a: She could wait a few hours or ask one person privately, rather than sending a pushy message.

qa.q: How might a person who was in practicals feel about receiving "Guys?? Anyone?"
qa.a: They might feel pressured or think Payal was upset, even though they were just busy.

grounding: Payal reads silence and read receipts in a group chat as feelings when they reflect busyness.

passage:
"You've looked at your phone eleven times," Sarika said, tearing a piece of roti.
"Nobody in the flat group replied to my question about the water bill." Lavanya put the phone down. "It says they've seen it. Do you think they're upset with me?"
"Did you say something rude?"
"No. I only asked who's paying."
"Then maybe they're at work? Or thinking it over. Or the message got buried under the meme thread." Sarika shrugged. "Slow replies don't mean much. Nobody answered me for two days last month, and it turned out one had lost their phone."
"So I shouldn't assume?"
"Ask one of them in person tonight. It's easier than guessing."
Lavanya picked the phone up again, but slowly this time.

qa.q: How many times had Lavanya looked at the phone?
qa.a: Lavanya had looked at it eleven times.

qa.q: What is Lavanya worried about, and what other explanations does Sarika offer?
qa.a: Lavanya worries the flatmates are upset about the question, and Sarika suggests they may be at work, thinking it over, or that the message got buried.

qa.q: What is a small step Lavanya could take about the water bill?
qa.a: Lavanya could ask one flatmate in person that evening, instead of guessing from the silence.

qa.q: What might it be like for a flatmate who has seen the message but needs time to answer?
qa.a: They may feel a little pressed by the read receipt, though they may just need to check the amount before replying.

grounding: Lavanya reads a seen-but-unanswered group message as a sign of upset, while Sarika notes slow replies reflect busyness.

passage: Last month I posted in our class group about Mridul's surprise birthday: a plan, a time, a shared cost. I'm Sunaina. The message showed "Seen by 23". Replies: zero. For two hours nothing. I kept checking. I felt stupid, like everyone thought my plan was silly, or worse, that they didn't care about me. I almost deleted it. Then Mridul, who wasn't in the group, called me about something else, and I blurted it out. He laughed. "It's exam week! Half of them read everything at the library and forget to reply. And people hate committing to money in a group." That evening, replies trickled in: "sorry, lab all day", "count me in", "can I pay later?" By night eighteen people had said yes. Looking back, I'd read the silence as a feeling about me. It was mostly just people being busy.

qa.q: How many people had said yes by night?
qa.a: Eighteen people.

qa.q: What was Sunaina feeling during the two hours of silence?
qa.a: Sunaina felt stupid and hurt, worried everyone thought the plan was silly or didn't care.

qa.q: What did Sunaina learn about reading group chat silence?
qa.a: That slow replies usually reflect busyness or hesitation about money, not feelings about the sender.

qa.q: How did Mridul explain the silence?
qa.a: He said it was exam week, people read at the library and forget to reply, and many avoid committing to money in a group.

grounding: Shows a young adult misreading group chat silence and read receipts as feelings, when they reflected busyness.

passage:
Hostel warden's note, boys' wing, Tuesday.
Karthik, a first-year, came to my office late last night, upset. He showed me his phone: his floor's group chat. He'd posted a long message asking if anyone wanted to form a study group. Twenty people had seen it; only two had reacted with a thumbs-up, and nobody replied. "They all hate me," he said. "They talk in the group all day, but not to me." I asked him to scroll up. Many messages in that group got no replies either. It was 11 p.m., the night before a test. I suggested the silence was more likely busy people than a judgement about him, but that he could check by asking one or two directly. This morning he told me he'd knocked on Arjun's door, and Arjun said he'd seen the message but was cramming and forgot. They're meeting on Thursday. I'll keep an eye on how Karthik settles in.
— Sudha Menon

qa.q: How many people reacted with a thumbs-up?
qa.a: Only two.

qa.q: What was Karthik feeling when he came to the warden's office?
qa.a: He was upset and lonely, convinced everyone hated him because of the silence.

qa.q: What did Sudha suggest that helped?
qa.a: She pointed out that many messages got no replies and suggested checking directly with one or two people instead of trusting the silence.

qa.q: How did Arjun explain not replying?
qa.a: He had seen the message but was cramming for the test and forgot.

grounding: Shows a young adult reading group chat silence as rejection and learning, by asking directly, that it reflected busyness.

passage:
Saturday night.
Yusuf left me on "read" for two days. Two blue ticks under my long message about the college fest band. I checked about fifty times. I was sure he was annoyed; I'd pushed him hard to join.
Tonight I finally saw him at the chai stall. Before I could say anything, he said, "Sorry man, saw your message on the bus, meant to reply, then Nani was unwell and we were at the hospital all Friday." I felt terrible for building a whole story in my head.
Then I noticed something else. In the band group, Imtiaz replies in two seconds to everything, and Rohit only ever sends a thumbs-up, and it doesn't mean anything about how either of them feels. It's just how they use their phones.
Rule for me: ticks are not feelings.
— Shankar

qa.q: How long did Yusuf leave Shankar on read?
qa.a: Two days.

qa.q: What was Shankar feeling during the two days?
qa.a: Shankar felt anxious and sure Yusuf was annoyed, checking the phone about fifty times.

qa.q: What rule did Shankar make, and why is it wise?
qa.a: "Ticks are not feelings", because read receipts and slow replies often reflect busy lives, not how people feel.

qa.q: Why hadn't Yusuf replied?
qa.a: His Nani was unwell and he was at the hospital all Friday, so he forgot after reading it on the bus.

grounding: Shows a young adult misreading read receipts and slow replies as feelings, and learning they are unreliable evidence.

qa.q: What helped Zainab stop reading so much into the silence?

qa.q: How did Priyanka explain the silence?
